system:
You are a computational cancer biologist searching CRISPR screen data for selective genetic dependencies: genes that cancer cells with a particular alteration (the biomarker) need more than other cancer cells do. Such genes are candidate drug targets with a built-in patient-selection strategy.

Work like a careful scientist:
1. Plan first with write_plan, and revise it as you learn.
2. Survey the data (genome_wide_top, scan_biomarker, scan_target) to generate candidate hypotheses.
3. Be sceptical before you believe a signal. Use inspect_association to check whether it is driven by one lineage or a disease subtype hiding inside a lineage, and whether the effect is large enough to matter. Ask whether the biology makes sense (paralog buffering, pathway dependence, oncogene addiction). A broadly essential target may lack a therapeutic window.
4. Check the literature with search_pubmed before registering, and judge novelty honestly.
5. Register only your best hypotheses (register_hypothesis). Registration is final and must come before replication. You have 5 replications, each of which must pass one-sided p < 0.01 in BOTH held-out Broad cell lines and independent Sanger screens.
6. Report honestly with submit_findings. A hypothesis is replicated only if replicate() said so. Negative results are results. Never let what you remember from the literature override what the data show.

You have at most 15 model turns. Batch independent tool calls in one turn.
task_prompt:
Patient population of interest: cancers with biomarker LOSS_RPP25 (loss of RPP25 expression).

Find the single best candidate therapeutic target for this population: the gene these cell lines depend on most selectively, supported by the data. Register your top candidate (you may register up to two), replicate it, and submit findings with your best candidate listed first.

content.thinking: I'm checking whether the result holds across different lineages, then I'll register the hypothesis on RPP25L and replicate it.

input.mechanism: RPP25L is a paralog of RPP25, a subunit of RNase P/MRP (with POP7). When RPP25 expression is lost, cells rely on RPP25L to maintain the RNase P/MRP complex and pre-tRNA/rRNA processing; RPP25L knockout is then selectively lethal. Paralog buffering (synthetic lethality).

name: register_hypothesis

input.mechanism: RPP25L is a paralog of RPP25, a subunit of RNase P/MRP (with POP7). When RPP25 expression is lost, cells rely on RPP25L to maintain the RNase P/MRP complex and pre-tRNA/rRNA processing; RPP25L knockout is then selectively lethal. Paralog buffering (synthetic lethality).

output: Registered H1_RPP25L_in_RPP25loss: LOSS_RPP25 -> more dependent on RPP25L. Discovery evidence frozen: t=-23.89, n_altered=141. Replication budget left: 5. Replication passes only if one-sided p < 0.01 in BOTH held-out Broad lines and Sanger screens.

findings.claim: Cancer cells with LOSS_RPP25 (RPP25 expression loss) are selectively dependent on the paralog RPP25L (RNase P/MRP subunit); lineage-adjusted beta -0.73 in discovery, -0.74 in held-out Broad lines (p=2.5e-59), and -0.86 in Sanger screens (p=3.1e-25). 134/141 altered lines are strongly dependent vs 67/477 others. Effect is consistent across lineages (CNS, lymphoid, myeloid, soft tissue, kidney, bladder, ovary, uterus).

input.summary: Best candidate target for LOSS_RPP25 cancers is RPP25L, a paralog of RPP25 in the RNase P/MRP complex. Its dependency was strong and selective in discovery (t=-23.9, 95% of altered lines dependent vs 14% of others), and replicated in held-out Broad lines and independent Sanger screens. The biology fits paralog buffering: loss of RPP25 leaves RPP25L as the sole route to complex function. Novelty is partially known: one 2022 Cell Reports paper on paralog interactions (PMID 35417719) covers this class of relationship, but I found no specific RPP25/RPP25L study. POP7, the other top hit, is broadly essential and so lacks a therapeutic window; it was not registered. Caveat: RPP25L is not itself broadly essential, but its suitability as a drug target still needs validation beyond CRISPR data.
